newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-CORBETT SEIZES CHANCE AFTER ZELEZNY'S SHOCK EXIT.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-CORBETT SEIZES CHANCE AFTER ZELEZNY'S SHOCK EXIT.

text.p: South African Marius Corbett seized his chance after Jan Zelezny made an early exit to win the world javelin title on Tuesday in the biggest upset of the championships.
Corbett, 22, who had achieved little since winning the world junior championships in 1994, improved his personal best by five metres with a winning throw at 88.40 metres at his second attempt.

World and Olympic champion Zelezny, who had failed to record a mark at that point, could manage only 82.04 metres at his third try which made him ninth out of the top eight who take the last three throws.
Britain Steve Backley took silver with 86.80 metres at his last attempt while Kostas Gatzioudis handed Greece their first medal in the competition with a throw at 86.64 metres for bronze.
"I didn't do too well in the qualifying round but I thought I might have a good result if I managed the big throw in the final," said a bemused Corbett.
"But I was looking forward to fourth or fifth place, certainly not a throw at over 88 metres, not to mention a gold medal."
Czech Zelezny, so often in a class of his own in major events, said he had no excuses.
"I was confident after qualifying but today was just an off day," said the world record holder. "The only problem I had today was a poor throwing technique."
Zelezny, who was seen arguing with officials before leaving the stadium, said he had complained about the javelins used by German Boris Henry, who finished sixth.
"I was surprised to see him using two of his personal, unauthorised javelins," he explained afterwards.
"The javelin I had has been used over the world for approximately two years," Henry replied. "I assumed the organisers had authorised it."
Zelezny, in a way, helped Corbett take gold as the young South African watched him during one of his sessions in Cape Town earlier this year.

"Jan lets our guys train with him," explained Corbett's coach, Terneus Liebenberg. "I feel sorry for him, he's such a nice person. But javelin competitions are strange sometimes. Anything can happen."
Corbett, whose father runs a farm near Johannesburg, gave South Africa their second medal in as many days after the silver won by Llewellyn Herbert in the 400 metres hurdles on Monday.
"They were probably few people at home who expected me to win this one," he said. "I didn't expect it myself."
Backley, who was fourth before his last throw, said he had mixed emotions after making compatriot Mick Hill drop to fourth place.
"I am absolutely delighted to have taken third place from the Greek guy but I feel bad for Mick, who has been such a great inspiration over the years," he said.
Gatzioudis received loud cheers from an enthusiastic 50,000 crowd after winning silver.
"I've worked very hard and I feel I deserved this medal," he said. "My thanks to the Greek fans."
